\\\"f551fa1f1e6213469c856a880839eefff504fb39f4dd692000b2df80a20a7f5e\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# K-SYS-014：推理服务恢复：提交边界、执行组与重试身份\\\\n\\\\n恢复首先要确定哪些工作已经成为外部可依赖的结果、哪些状态仍可信，以及谁有权继续提交。检测到超时或重新启动进程，都不能独立回答这些问题。\\\\n\\\\n## 三个边界分别记录\\\\n\\\\n计算边界表示哪些输入位置已经生成完整模型状态；确认边界表示投机/搜索后哪些 token 属于保留路径；外部提交边界表示服务已经按协议发布的内容。它们可能不同。prefill 末行可以产生一个 token，但该 token 自身的 KV 未必已经计算；网络发送返回也不等于客户端已消费。\\\\n\\\\n恢复描述至少包含请求与尝试身份、模型/adapter/输入配置、已确认 token、可重建的共同状态位置，以及需要继续的随机、grammar 和输出状态。只保存 KV 字节无法恢复任意请求；只保存 token 也不自动恢复任意递归模型、分支状态或已经发生的外部动作。\\\\n\\\\n可重算的模型状态与不可重复的业务结果分开处理。固定前缀可以帮助重建 KV，但跨 backend 重算是否逐位一致取决于数值契约。若协议需要断线续传，应有明确的游标、去重与确认规则；否则应报告失败或重新请求，不能默认已经获得“恰好一次”交付。\\\\n\\\\n## 故障矩阵决定恢复路线\\\\n\\\\n| 故障位置 | 首先确认 | 合法的恢复或终止方式 |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| 输入处理进程失败 | 是否已准入、输入是否可重放 | 从固定输入重做未提交部分，清理预留 |\\\\n| 单个计算 rank 退出 | 执行组是否还拥有一致状态 | 停止受影响组，从共同提交点重建或明确失败 |\\\\n| KV 传输部分完成 | 目标范围和源副本的有效性 | 撤销未提交目标，重传或从可恢复前缀重算 |\\\\n| 源在接管期间失效 | 目标是否完成且已获提交权 | 按协议完成接管；否则使用其他副本或重建 |\\\\n| 磁盘/压缩读取失败 | 哪些对象可重建、哪些记录必须保留 | 失效对应缓存；不能把未完成解码当作可用状态 |\\\\n| 客户端断线 | 哪些内容已发出、协议能否确认消费 | 依协议取消、续传或失败，不猜测客户端进度 |\\\\n\\\\n每条路线同时说明输出处理和资源清理。最后一个错误通常只是连锁超时，诊断要保留最早失败、rank 状态、操作序号和已经完成的范围。\\\\n\\\\n## 执行组恢复与单请求恢复不同\\\\n\\\\nTP/EP 等组内的 ranks 必须执行相容的操作序列。一个 rank 的失败不能让其他 ranks 继续把局部结果当作完整层；请求取消也不能让某个 rank 单独跳过 collective。根据固定通信库的错误处理契约终止或重建受影响资源，并让调度器停止向失效组提交新工作。\\\\n\\\\n重建可以重新加载模型、重建 communicator/执行上下文，再恢复合法状态。已经失效的设备句柄、注册区、页表和图对象不能仅因地址看起来相同就继续使用。较大的执行组能处理更大模型，但故障影响范围与恢复时间也随组织方式改变。\\\\n\\\\n## 迁移期间只允许一份提交权\\\\n\\\\n[Llumnix v1](../sources/S-LLUMNIX.md) §4.2 描述了分阶段复制、目标预留和迁移异常处理；它利用 append-only KV 隐藏部分复制时间。窗口覆盖、递归状态和可回滚分支不自动满足这个前提，需冻结或另行保存恢复版本。\\\\n\\\\n应用需要明确源端何时停止提交、目标何时获得提交权，以及确认丢失时如何判断。新尝试带独立代次，旧节点的迟到消息不能重新获得当前请求的提交权。多个控制节点也必须提供一致的授权规则，不能各自根据本地超时决定同时接管。\\\\n\\\\n最后源副本释放与目标提交之间的窗口必须有恢复依据。可以保留源直到确认、依赖已经完整的其他副本，或允许从持久输入重算；选择取决于故障模型与成本。内存内迁移本身不能保证机器同时失效后仍有持久恢复能力。\\\\n\\\\n## 重试预算和过载反馈\\\\n\\\\n重试可能与原任务同时消耗资源，且常发生在系统已过载时。控制并发尝试、总时间预算和退避，避免把一次网络或节点故障变成请求放大。幂等传输 ID 处理重复范围，逻辑请求 ID 处理重复提交；它们是不同层次。\\\\n\\\\n恢复后需重新检查 deadline、质量和容量。如果剩余时间已无法满足任务，不应无条件重试直到某次成功再隐藏此前失败。故障恢复实验与正常稳态性能分开报告，也要度量恢复期间对其他请求造成的影响。\\\\n\\\\n## 验证可观察的不变量\\\\n\\\\n在预留后、部分传输后、目标发布前后、输出提交前后分别注入失败。检查请求终态唯一、输出序号连续、旧代次不覆盖新状态、未完成缓冲不被复用，以及资源最终回到声明的稳态基线。对随机生成，明确要求相同轨迹还是相同分布；对可重算缓存，检查恢复位置和其他状态族的交集。\\\\n\\\\n低失败率、短请求可能适合失败后重做；长请求、严格交互连续性或昂贵状态可能需要更多检查点、副本与接管协议。多种方案都要把恢复成本计入 SLO 与容量，而不是只比较无故障时的速度。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- infraagents:provenance -->\\\\n\\\\n## 来源与推导\\\\n\\\\n- [S-LLUMNIX：Llumnix](../sources/S-LLUMNIX.md)：§4 通过分阶段 append-only KV \\\"0ca7501a80e750152a5fb3b9815c77f9e3f9aa393ff7546b3f05375958f88606\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# K-SYS-016：租户隔离：资源份额、缓存命名空间与故障边界\\\\n\\\\n一个推理租户可以同时消耗 CPU、设备计算、KV 容量、adapter 驻留、网络、I/O 与响应缓冲。隔离设计应分别说明谁能够访问哪些对象、谁最多占用多少资源、谁在竞争时优先推进，以及一个故障影响哪些请求。限制其中一项不会自动建立其他保证。\\\\n\\\\n## 从入口身份传到状态拥有者\\\\n\\\\n入口确定的租户、模型/adapter 版本和请求身份，需要传递到调度、缓存、传输与输出。不同租户即使提交相同文本，也不默认取得对方的 KV、检索内容、adapter 或 trace。共享不可变公共前缀应以明确的公共对象契约和版本身份为前提，而不是通过发现相同 hash 就绕过授权。\\\\n\\\\n请求 ID 本身不是访问凭证。对共享缓存，授权范围与数值兼容性同时满足才允许命中；页句柄、远端地址和日志引用也不能只依赖可猜的槽号。过期版本退出目录后，在途访问仍要结束，最后回收时清除对新拥有者不应暴露的内容或重新初始化全部可读范围。\\\\n\\\\ntrace 保存排队、形状、长度、代次与资源事件通常已足以做归因。确需记录原始输入或输出时，把存取范围、保留时间和删除责任纳入同一对象生命周期。租户隔离不是要求所有状态复制一份，而是要求共享的条件和可见范围可验证。\\\\n\\\\n## 主机限额的实际含义\\\\n\\\\n[Linux 6.12 cgroup v2](../sources/S-LINUX-RESOURCES.md) 区分权重、上限、保护与独占分配。CPU 权重决定竞争时的相对份额，CPU 带宽上限约束一段时间可消耗的执行时间，cpuset 约束可运行的 CPU/内存节点；它们不能互相替代。CPU 配额不保证独占 cache、内存带宽或确定的尾延迟。\\\\n\\\\nmemory.high 会引入回收压力和节流，memory.max 在无法回收时可触发 cgroup 内 OOM；文件页缓存、匿名内存与部分内核/网络缓冲也可能计入预算。只统计模型 tensor 会遗漏这些消耗。内存控制器不是所有 GPU 显存对象的自动配额器，GPU 容量仍需执行器和实际设备机制约束。RDMA 对象数、线程/进程数量与存储流量也可能先于字节预算耗尽。\\\\n\\\\n## GPU 共享必须绑定具体机制\\\\n\\\\n下列界限取自固定的 [NVIDIA device plugin v0.16.1](../sources/S-NVIDIA-PLUGIN.md) README。这里说明该版本公开的资源与部署契约，不把插件文档扩展成所有设备、驱动或攻击场景的安全证明。\\\\n\\\\n| 机制 | 该来源明确支持的理解 | 不能由资源名称推出的保证 |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| 整卡分配 | 将指定设备暴露给容器，区分 UUID/index 等身份传递方式 | 其他宿主进程是否仍可访问、整机故障是否隔离 |\\\\n| CUDA time-slicing | 多个访问份额指向同一底层 GPU；文档明确没有额外的显存与故障域隔离 | 每份额对应固定显存或固定吞吐；申请更多份额按比例得到算力 |\\\\n| 插件的 MPS 共享 | 控制进程按份额限制客户端可用显存与计算能力；该版本只支持完整 GPU，并不支持启用 MIG 的设备 | 与独占物理设备相同的尾延迟、性能无干扰或覆盖所有错误的隔离 |\\\\n| MIG 资源暴露 | 在硬件支持前提下，none/single/mixed 策略决定暴露方式；mixed 可暴露按 profile 命名的资源 | 任意 profile 组合均合法、profile 吞吐线性缩放，或共享宿主/网络/供电故障自动消失 |\\\\n\\\\nMIG、MPS 与 time-slicing 不应被合并成一个“虚拟 GPU”容量数字。MIG profile 需要对应实际硬件支持与配置，多个访问份额也可能继续共享同一 MIG 资源。更细的硬件隔离承诺需要相应固定硬件文档和故障测试；本章不从插件的资源暴露推断未记录的保证。\\\\n\\\\n## 容量、公平与故障预算\\\\n\\\\n设定共享设备的 KV 池为 8 GiB，租户 A/B 各保留 3 GiB，另有 2 GiB 可借用池。借用可在空闲时增加利用率，但 A 已有活跃请求占用的借用状态，不能在 B 到来时立即按账面扣回；必须有合法结束、迁移、重算或拒绝路线。仅设“每租户 10 请求”的限额，会让长上下文租户占据远多于短请求租户的容量。\\\\n\\\\n再设一张卡被 time-slicing 暴露为 8 份。接收 8 个各需要 10 GiB 的服务进程，不会把物理显存变成 80 GiB。共享份额数量只允许更多访问者，模型加载和峰值容量仍需真实字节账。同样，空闲时一个租户借到更多设备时间，不代表竞争时能继续获得相同服务率。\\\\n\\\\n## 验证与选择改变\\\\n\\\\n构造两租户相同输入但不同权限/adapter 的请求，检查缓存、结果、日志与迟到消息无越界归属；再让一个租户持续增长 KV、生成超长响应、启动大量冷 adapter、消耗 CPU 配额与存储流量。观察另一个租户的准入、尾延迟和可完成工作量，不能只检查进程没有退出。\\\\n\\\\n故障测试按已承诺的边界设计：终止一个 worker、制造配额内存不足、使一个共享设备不可用或让网络中断，确认影响范围、可重试语义和清理责任。对全卡故障、宿主故障与租户进程错误分别记录，不能把某一种测试通过推广到全部错误。\\\\n\\\\n严格隔离需求可能要求独占设备或独立执行域；低占用且允许干扰的服务可采用共享。统一基座内的多租户执行节省内存，却把应用调度器变成主要容量和身份边界，必须同时有明确的资源账与独立污染测试。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- \\\"1b9dcfd5fea499a91611459bb936e1c1c49ceb562171fb0f1ba360a7010f5d32\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# K-ALG-023：请求路由与迁移：命中收益、排队和追赶条件\\\\n\\\\n路由选择请求去哪里执行，迁移允许在实际状态增长后重新选择。两者应最小化与任务有关的完整代价，并保持输入、状态和输出提交的一致性。\\\\n\\\\n## 命中最多的节点未必最早完成\\\\n\\\\n候选节点的估计成本可以包括排队、未命中输入计算、远端读取/转换、执行阶段和接管开销。缓存身份先满足语义，再比较性能；过期目录与滞后的负载报告不能直接作为执行许可。\\\\n\\\\n设定 A 有本地前缀，排队 100 ms、剩余计算 10 ms；B 无缓存但无排队，重算 80 ms；C 排队 10 ms，远端取得正确状态需 40 ms、剩余计算 10 ms。对应估计为 110、80、60 ms，C 才是这一设定下较好的选择。若 C 的目标容量或状态身份检查失败，它必须退出合法候选集合，不能仅凭最低分数继续接收。\\\\n\\\\n最短请求队列、最少 token、最少内存占用与最短完成时间也不等价。长历史会增加 KV 和 attention，长输出决定未来驻留，prefill 与 decode 的资源需求不同。未知输出可以使用有范围的估计，但实际准入仍需检查当前资源和近期增量。\\\\n\\\\n## 全局观察与本地决定\\\\n\\\\n[Mooncake](../sources/S-MOONCAKE.md) §5–6 将缓存局部性、池负载与 SLO 联合调度；[Llumnix](../sources/S-LLUMNIX.md) §4 将全局实例配对与本地请求选择分开，并用虚拟使用量表达多种调度目标。这些是减少全局跟踪成本的候选组织，不保证一个内存标量就能预测所有延迟。\\\\n\\\\n多个路由器同时看到同一个空闲节点，可能把下一批请求全部送过去。预留、局部再检查和适度分散可以减少这种竞争，但需要说明何时释放预留与如何拒绝过时决定。负载报告越稀疏，控制开销越低，决策误差可能越大；频繁迁移又会放大网络和状态成本。\\\\n\\\\n## 活跃迁移的追赶条件\\\\n\\\\n对可冻结旧前缀且仅追加新状态的请求，可以一边复制旧状态一边生成新 token，随后复制增量，最后短暂停止源端推进并移交尾部。对可变窗口、递归覆盖或投机回滚，必须另行定义每一阶段的快照边界。\\\\n\\\\n设初始状态 D、持续新增速度 g、有效复制速度 B，忽略其他开销，首阶段耗时 D/B，产生增量 D·g/B；下一阶段的增量继续乘 g/B。只有 B>g 才有这种几何收敛机会。实际链路竞争、不同块开销与生成速度波动都可能打破估计，因此应有停止追赶、暂停复制或中止迁移的条件。\\\\n\\\\n设定一个请求组有 1000 MiB 待迁移，新增 10 MiB/s，复制 100 MiB/s。前三阶段分别约 10、1、0.1 秒，剩余增量为 1 MiB，最终停顿复制约 10 ms，另加提交开销。总迁移时间约 11.11 秒，不能用 10 ms 停顿代表整个迁移免费。如果可用带宽降到 8 MiB/s，小于新增速度，继续原策略不会追上。\\\\n\\\\n## 目标容量、输出与网络的共同预算\\\\n\\\\n目标在每阶段接收前预留必要空间；源在迁移中完成、取消或被抢占时，目的端清理未提交预留。移交时明确最后确认 token、已计算状态与已经发布输出，防止新旧端重复发送或遗漏。数据传输和请求接管的责任见 [恢复协议](../system-semantics/serving-recovery.md)。\\\\n\\\\n迁移可以释放某实例空间、减轻干扰、支持优先级或排空，但同时会占用目的容量和网络。搬走一个大请求可能比重新路由未来请求更昂贵；搬走多个小请求也可能增加控制开销。比较预计避免的等待/抢占成本与迁移全过程成本，并保留足够收益余量，避免围绕预测噪声来回迁移。\\\\n\\\\n## 热点副本与优先级\\\\n\\\\n复制热门前缀把后续请求分散到多个实例，可以同时改善命中与排队；也可能将有限缓存装满同一热点，挤出其他高价值对象。高优先级请求可通过迁走同驻请求获得资源，但被迁请求的等待和 SLO 仍需要记录。总体 goodput 上升不代表每个租户都改善。\\\\n\\\\n验证使用热点逐渐变化、长短请求混合、负载报告延迟和带宽下降的轨迹；同时观察排队、重算、迁移字节、停顿、拒绝、内存碎片与各类 SLO。若节省的计算小于新增排队，或迁移长期追不上，路由应允许回到简单分散或本地重算方案。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- infraagents:provenance -->\\\\n\\\\n## 来源与推导\\\\n\\\\n- logprobs、分支或投机验证时，所需行集合另行表达，不能复用这个简化规则。\\\\n\\\\n设 q=[2,5,3]，则 p=[0,2,7,10]，三个末位置行是 [1,6,9]。若请求被重排，必须同时重排身份映射、位置与结果路由；shape 正确不能发现把第 6 行交给另一请求的错误。\\\\n\\\\n```pseudocode\\\\n更新本轮有效请求集合，保存每个物理槽对应的逻辑身份和代次\\\\n按所选表示生成 query 位置、输入 token 与缓存写入位置\\\\n建立输出行到请求/位置/分支的映射，再提交设备计算\\\\n按该轮映射解释 logits 和采样结果，校验返回代次\\\\n最后消费者完成后才覆盖本轮输入、metadata 或辅助缓冲\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## 压紧与固定容量的交换\\\\n\\\\n压紧减少无效行，却付出收集、前缀和、重排或 metadata 更新；固定槽与图桶方便稳定地址和复用，但可能计算填充行并增加多桶驻留。[已核对的执行器实例](../sources/S-VLLM-RUNNER.md) 维护持久批状态，再压紧本轮 query；它说明这两个选择可以组合，并不要求独立引擎复制同一类结构。\\\\n\\\\n容量 16 的桶承载 10 个有效行时，有 6/16=37.5% 的槽位未承载有效行；这只是槽位比例，不直接等于浪费的运行时间。是否跳过无效行、kernel 效率和图重放成本决定实际收益。若每步都重新整理大块历史，压紧的准备成本也可能超过避免的填充工作。\\\\n\\\\n## 用映射与完成证据区分解释\\\\n\\\\n同一请求单独执行、混合批执行、行重排和取消后复用槽位，应得到相同语义结果。记录每轮身份、绝对位置、缓存槽和 logits 路由，可将错配与模型数值误差分开。延迟设备完成再安排下一轮，能检查固定地址是否被过早覆盖。比较准备、设备、采样与可见输出的完整时间线，避免把省下提交工作误当作数学计算变少。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- extracted-character range 0:6538]\\\\n# K-SYS-008：服务协议：接收、流式背压与终止语义\\\\n\\\\n推理服务将内部生成状态映射为可观察的网络事件；接收、执行完成和客户端收到结果是不同的完成点。\\\\n\\\\n## 问题、不变量与设计轴\\\\n\\\\n问题：生成是逐 token 产生、可能很长、可被中途放弃的过程，而客户端通过有限带宽、会断开、会重试的连接消费它。协议层要回答的是\\\\\\\"一个请求在外部有哪些可观察状态，内容以什么粒度交付，客户端慢或消失时内部资源怎样受约束，重试时什么算同一个请求\\\\\\\"。\\\\n\\\\n不变量：每个对外事件都能映射到确定的内部状态（已接收、已准入、首内容、终止原因）；交付的内容与模型输出的 token 序列按约定的切分一一对应；发送缓冲有界，慢客户端不能无限占用主机内存或拖住设备侧进度；终止（完成、取消、错误、超时）各自有明确的资源回收路径；重试身份使重复提交不被当成两条独立请求。\\\\n\\\\n成本项：每事件的序列化与系统调用、发送缓冲驻留、连接数对执行域的占用、背压传播到调度器的延迟、以及为\\\\\\\"恰好一次交付\\\\\\\"保存的提交记录。\\\\n\\\\n设计轴：内容粒度（逐 token / 按时间窗合并 / 按语义块）；背压位置（协议层丢弃 / 暂停生成 / 准入拒绝）；终止语义（取消即停 / 排空后停 / 允许迟到结果）；兼容目标（既有 API 子集 / 自定义协议）；重试身份（客户端 ID / 服务端幂等键 / 无）。SSE 流式加有界队列是常见的一点；无流式整段返回在短输出场景同样合法。轴上未列点同样合法。\\\\n\\\\n## 使用场景与协议选择\\\\n\\\\n设计对外接口、接入真实客户端，或探索流式输出、取消、会话续接与滚动更新时，需要解释用户能够观察到什么。目标协议的版本及支持子集、模型/前处理身份、输入输出范围、客户端消费方式和重试要求，共同决定输入解释、内容事件、终止原因与资源责任。哪些行为属于交付要求由当前任务决定；请求身份与执行完成的关系分别见 [请求身份](request-batch-identity.md) 和 [取消与完成](cancellation-resource-completion.md)。\\\\n\\\\n一次请求只在全部计算结束后返回结果时，普通请求—响应可以保持较简单的交付语义，但用户无法观察中间内容；需要逐步交付文本、音频或进度时，可以采用明确事件格式的 HTTP 流；需要在同一连接上持续输入、打断和接收内容时，可以选择 WebSocket 或另一种明确支持双向通信的协议。选择双向连接不会自动提供会话一致性，选择流式传输也不会自动降低模型的首内容计算时间。\\\\n\\\\n本地 ASGI 规范区分 HTTP 的单请求 scope 与 WebSocket 的连接 scope。同一 HTTP/2 连接可以承载多个请求，不能用连接身份代替请求身份；一个 WebSocket 会话内若有多个任务，也要定义各自的请求、回合和输出归属。协议版本、服务声明支持的行为与模型版本应分别识别。\\\\n\\\\n## 一条请求的外部状态\\\\n\\\\n参数验证、排队接收、开始执行、产生首个有效内容、持续输出、最终终止构成可观察协议。返回 HTTP 成功状态通常只说明响应开始，后续流仍可能失败。每条流需要明确的终止事件和原因，否则客户端无法区分正常结束与连接中断。\\\\n\\\\n流式 chunk 是传输单位，不一定是模型 token。一个 chunk 可包含多个 token、空角色信息或 usage 元数据；TTFT 应绑定协议定义的首个内容事件。压缩、代理缓冲和客户端解析还会改变收到事件的时间。\\\\n\\\\n固定 ASGI 规范要求：成功处理 http.response.body 的 send 返回时，本次 body 已交给服务器发送缓冲；它没有确认远端应用已经消费。http.response.start 没有同样的即时 flush 要求，服务器可以等到第一次 Response Body 再发送响应头。生成、交给发送缓冲和客户端收到是可分别观察的事件；它们可以发生在同一调用链，也可以跨越线程或进程，不据此要求引擎拆成固定组件。\\\\n\\\\n## 背压的资源含义\\\\n\\\\n若生成快于客户端消费，输出队列增长。无限队列让慢客户端持有大量文本/音频和请求状态，最终影响其他用户。限制队列、暂停后续生成或断开超时消费者是不同服务策略，应该由延迟与可靠性目标决定。\\\\n\\\\n暂停生成并不一定能释放 KV；完整请求状态仍需保留。对音频，过大队列还增加用户打断后的尾音。背压因此既是网络机制，也是调度和容量变量。\\\\n\\\\n## 取消、错误和重试\\\\n\\\\n客户端断开、发送失败、内部超时和模型异常都应进入同一请求终止账务，避免重复释放。重试是否允许复用请求 ID、是否可能重复输出、是否支持恢复已确认前缀，是协议明确承诺的功能，不能由客户端盲目重发推断。\\\\n\\\\n请求追踪可以跨 API、tokenizer、scheduler、runner 和输出阶段传播上下文。batch 是多请求聚合，需额外记录请求与执行批的映射。敏感原始输入不必全部写 trace，状态身份和摘要即可支持许多因果分析。\\\\n\\\\n## 兼容 API 的实际含义\\\\n\\\\n字段名字相同只说明表面结构。采样默认值、token 计数、流式 delta、工具调用结构、错误格式、取消和结束原因共同定义行为兼容。服务验收应以具体协议的输入输出实例和状态转换为准。内部 engine 能生成文本，与一个完整可消费的服务接口之间还有这些确定的语义关系。\\\\n\\\\n## 接收协议要连接实际执行域\\\\n\\\\n入口事件循环将请求交给分词线程/进程、调度器和模型 worker 时，每条队列都应携带请求版本、deadline、取消状态和缓冲所有权。[主机运行时](host-runtime.md)比较执行域组织；在协议层，关键是队列满时能明确等待、拒绝或终止，而不是已经接受后无限隐藏排队。\\\\n\\\\n租户限额应同时覆盖输入字节/长度、待处理工作、活跃状态和输出积压。只限制连接数不能阻止单连接携带大输入，按请求数平均也不能限制长上下文 KV。配额不足和模型版本未就绪可以有不同的可重试语义，错误响应需说明这次请求是否已经被接收及是否已有对外结果。\\\\n\\\\n## 滚动发布与连接生命周期\\\\n\\\\n服务发现和路由将新请求绑定到具体就绪版本；已有流式连接保持其请求版本和提交顺序。滚动发布先撤销旧实例的新准入，再排空或按明确协议迁移；关闭监听端口不等于现有生成、IPC 和设备操作全部结束。遇到最长排空时间时，最终错误或恢复能力必须与客户端契约一致。\\\\n\\\\n重试协议需要明确请求身份与去重范围。如果服务只能重新执行，就应披露可能重复已产生的内容；若支持从已确认位置恢复，还需保存对应模型、输入、采样/约束状态和输出序号。内部算子重新计算的幂等性不能自动提供网络交付的恰好一次语义。\\\\n\\\\n## 服务故障状态验证\\\\n\\\\n从参数验证前、进入队列后、首内容前、已交付若干内容后、最终结果已计算但未发送等边界分别断开连接或终止 worker。逐项核对客户端看到的事件、服务端提交记录、可否重试与最终资源账。慢客户端测试需要同时运行正常客户端，检查背压是否限定在预定队列和租户范围内。\\\\n\\\\n发布测试保留一条旧版本长流，切换新请求到新版本，再注入新实例预热失败和旧实例排空超时。成功条件包括结果版本可识别、未就绪实例不被路由、每条流有可解释终态、没有迟到旧消息污染新连接。TTFT 继续以首个有效内容计算，不能因发布期间先发空 chunk 就宣称满足目标。\\\\n\\\\n## 参数、计数与内容如何保持同一语义\\\\n\\\\n输入适配应明确缺省值、显式空值与非法值分别意味着什么。最大输出 token 数与“输入加输出”的上下文上限不是同一个数；文本输入的 token 数依赖固定 tokenizer、模板及特殊 token 规则。若外部接口支持 token ID 和文本两条入口，还要说明它们怎样形成相同的规范化输入，避免模板或特殊 token 被重复应用。相关推导见 [Tokenizer 与 I/O](tokenization-io.md)。\\\\n\\\\n采样、停止条件和结构化输出能力按声明的子集处理。未实现的参数应被明确拒绝或按已披露规则处理，不能仅因为字段能够解析就声称支持。停止序列可能跨越多个 token 或传输 chunk；如果协议规定不向用户展示停止文本，输出层需要保留足够的待确认内容，并将该缓冲延迟计入可见时间。流式与非流式的最终内容应在同一停止规则下比较。\\\\n\\\\n输出账应分别记录模型生成、正式提交和客户端收到的范围。usage 信息可以有自己的计数定义，但必须说明是否包含被丢弃的候选、停止内容或取消后的在途计算。不能以“模型执行过多少 token”替代用户收到的内容，也不能因为最终字符串一致就省略流内重复和乱序检查。\\\\n\\\\n## 一个慢客户端的容量算例\\\\n\\\\n以下参数全部为设定，不是服务实测。观察引擎到传输适配层之间的一处有界队列，假设编码后字节的实际入队速率为 8000 B/s，下游从这处队列的实际出队速率为 2000 B/s，允许积压 64 KiB，初始积压为零。在两种速率暂时保持不变、忽略额外封包开销的条件下，队列净增长为 6000 B/s，达到上限所需时间为\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\[\\\\nt_{\\\\\\\\mathrm{full}}=\\\\\\\\frac{65{,}536\\\\\\\\ \\\\\\\\mathrm{B}}{(8000-2000)\\\\\\\\ \\\\\\\\mathrm{B/s}}\\\\\\\\approx10.92\\\\\\\\ \\\\\\\\mathrm{s}.\\\\n\\\\\\\\]\\\\n\\\\n远端客户端消费 2000 B/s 本身不足以推出这个本地出队速率：下游发送缓冲仍有空间时，可以先吸收更多字节。只有背压已传导到这处队列，并在观察窗口确认其出队速率时，才能将相应值用于此式；端到端积压还需计入其他缓冲。\\\\n\\\\n若 128 个请求都达到该上限，仅这个输出层就保留 8 MiB。若每个暂停请求另占 6 MiB 私有模型状态，则还有 768 MiB 状态驻留；该状态大小是独立设定，不能由输出字节数推算。发送缓冲、序列化副本和共享前缀还应另按实际所有权计账。\\\\n\\\\n因此可以比较三个合法候选：持续暂停直到消费者恢复，限制暂停时间后终止，或采用任务允许的其他交付方式。暂停保留继续服务的机会，却延长状态占用；超时终止释放未来工作，但必须披露用户可见失败；默默丢弃未声明可丢弃的生成内容会改变任务。选择反转取决于客户端恢复分布、请求价值、资源压力和服务承诺。\\\\n\\\\n验证预测包括队列在达到额度前的增长斜率、饱和后的生成节奏、取消后的在途消耗，以及正常客户端是否受到额外影响。分别观察引擎出队、服务器发送和客户端读取，可以避免把不同缓冲边界的速率与完成事件混用。\\\\n\\\\n## 验收必须包含未完成和被拒绝的请求\\\\n\\\\n局部协议检查覆盖参数、默认值、事件格式、结束原因和解析边界；集成检查覆盖模板到模型输入的映射、增量到最终内容的重建、断开与内部取消的联系。系统检查则使用实际到达过程、混合长度、慢消费者、取消和版本更新，观察完整请求集合与资源变化。\\\\n\\\\n例如一个设定的 10 s 测量窗口内发出 100 个请求，10 个被拒绝，90 个获接收，其中 80 个在窗口内完成、10 个仍未完成；已完成请求中有 72 个同时满足任务规定的质量与全部时延约束。按此窗口和该任务的合格定义，合格完成率为 7.2 请求/s，合格请求占全部发出请求的比例为 72%。这两个量不同，且均不能通过只保留 80 个完成请求来重新定义分母。窗口结束后应继续记录尚未完成请求的结局，排空阶段与稳态窗口分别标明。\\\\n\\\\n固定 GenAI-Perf 文档把 goodput 定义为满足指标约束的完成请求率；如果任务还要求质量或协议正确性，就要把额外门限明确加入资格定义。其 README 将 TTFT 写为首个 response，当前任务若采用首个有效内容，必须核对哪些流事件被解析器计入，保留空事件、首内容与终态的区别。修改刷新频率、代理缓冲或流事件格式后，应重新确认该映射，不能仅比较同名指标字段。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"# K-TOOLS-006：正确性 Oracle：函数参考、状态变形与服务契约\\\\n\\\\n正确性验证需要一组互补的 oracle：数值函数、状态转换、采样分布和外部协议分别有可检查的关系。\\\\n\\\\n## 函数参考与实现独立性\\\\n\\\\n简单稠密 attention、高精度矩阵路径或原模型 forward 可以作为数值参考，前提是输入、mask、位置和权重一致。参考若调用与被测实现相同的页表索引或共享同一个错误 processor，就失去对应维度的独立性。独立性应具体说明到逻辑组件，而不是仅说“另一个测试”。\\\\n\\\\n## 变形关系覆盖状态\\\\n\\\\n同一请求独立执行与放入不同顺序的 batch 应保持规定语义；整段 prefill 与分块 prefill 应一致；冷缓存与合法前缀命中后继续应一致；页的物理重新排列不应改变逻辑结果。这些关系改变执行组织而保持函数，适合在 CPU 小实例上穷举边界。\\\\n\\\\n取消后，新请求使用回收槽应与全新槽执行一致；两个不同 adapter 的相同 prompt 应分别对应各自参考；window rollover 前后应对应同一绝对位置定义。每种关系都来自具体状态模型，可以发现“常见样例都对”时仍隐藏的错误。\\\\n\\\\n## 概率与协议需要其他 Oracle\\\\n\\\\n随机采样用固定小分布检验支持集、归一化和频率，投机检验目标分布关系；单条文本 exact match 不足以证明概率正确。服务协议检查 chunk 顺序、终止事件、stop string、usage、错误和背压，不能只看返回了 HTTP 200。\\\\n\\\\n质量指标还包括 ASR 词错误率、视觉任务准确性、图像质量或语音一致性。数值近似通过小张量容差与任务质量合格各提供不同支持。一个完整工程验收把这些 oracle 组合起来，而不是让一个最终布尔值遮住具体覆盖。\\\\n\\\\n## 组合覆盖来自相交的状态边界\\\\n\\\\n各机制单独正确，不能推出组合正确。先列出它们共同触及的对象：分页与前缀共享共同管理尾块；投机与 grammar 共同管理未提交分支；异步执行与取消共同管理在途缓冲；量化与迁移共同管理尺度与布局。测试应覆盖交界上的状态转换，而不是机械地对全部参数做笛卡尔积。\\\\n\\\\n例如“前缀共享＋异步取消”的判别场景：A/B 共享完整前缀，各自追加不同 token；取消 A 后立即把它可回收的私有槽分给 C；延迟 A 的完成通知；继续 B/C。参考分别从各自逻辑 token 全量重建，检查 B 未被污染、C 不接收 A 的迟到输出、共享页未提前回收。这个时序可以区分身份错误、引用错误和完成事件错误。\\\\n\\\\n## 性质测试与并发调度\\\\n\\\\n把物理页排列、batch 排序、分块边界和无关请求插入作为变形维度，保持模型函数与有效输入不变。生成器需要包含跨页、非整除尾部、零长度边界和最大合法范围，并在失败时保留最小可复现输入。变形关系本身也要有前提：改变采样种子不要求文本一致，改变模型版本不再保证缓存等价。\\\\n\\\\n并发测试要控制完成顺序，包括旧工作晚于新工作返回、多个 stream 的不同事件次序、传输部分完成、取消与提交竞争。随机压力有发现价值，确定性的受控时序更便于解释；两者都不能以一次未出现错误证明所有竞态已消除。\\\\n\\\\n## 长时间运行检查守恒关系\\\\n\\\\n资源池满足总量=空闲+活跃占用+在途保护+保留但可解释的占用，各项不能重复计数。测试经过多轮分配、共享、驱逐、取消和失败恢复后，未完成工作清空时应回到预先声明的稳态基线。缓存刻意保留导致的驻留与不可达对象泄漏不同；观察 RSS 不下降时，需要先区分 allocator 保留和真实失去所有者。\\\\n\\\\n同时检查请求终态唯一性、输出序号连续性、最多一次的外部提交，以及失败是否留下可复用却未初始化的块。故障注入应落在定义过的协议边界；若业务允许重试，参考需要包含重试身份与结果提交规则，不能用最终“有输出”掩盖重复响应。\\\\n\\\\n## 独立保留验证检查什么\\\\n\\\\n开发样例用于定位和调参，最终保留样例覆盖未参与选择的形状、长度、输入分层和状态时序。对低位路径，先用固定量化参数的独立公式排除实现错误，再检查原模型质量；对概率路径，先用小分布验证采样关系，再做统计检验。独立性说明到具体组件：参考可以共用权重文件，但不能在要验证页表索引时共用被测页表逻辑。\\\\n\\\\n知识章节提出的是 oracle 和区分实验。只有实际任务执行这些检查，才能记录相应通过或失败；章节写得完整、结构检查通过，都不能被标记成目标引擎的正确性证据。\\\\n\\\\n## 从任务要求派生检查，而不改变要求\\\\n\\\\n先区分用户契约、组件数学定义和本次测试实现。用户要求完整历史或精确输出时，测试驱动不能为了可运行而截短历史、忽略出错请求或改成更宽松的质量定义。测试参考和观测器可以修订，但修订说明应回答原检查错在何处、新检查如何恢复原契约、哪些旧结论受到影响。\\\\n\\\\n构建初期没有现成生产引擎可以作为唯一 oracle 时，按可独立核对的边界建立组合参考：固定权重与前处理下的函数参考；小状态空间中的索引/所有权关系；端到端协议与任务质量。组件参考只覆盖其声明的域，不会因局部结果正确而自动补齐整个服务的验证。接口问题分别见 [服务协议](../system-semantics/service-protocol.md)、[请求身份](../system-semantics/request-batch-identity.md) 与 [取消和完成](../system-semantics/cancellation-resource-completion.md)；张量语义见 [基础算子](../algorithms/operator-primitives.md) 和 [后端选择](../frameworks/attention-backends.md)。\\\\n\\\\n## 验证器也要能拒绝已知错误\\\\n\\\\n这里的负对照是主动构造一个违反既定要求的输出或轨迹，检查验证器是否确实拒绝；它检验的是测试辨别力，不是目标引擎性能。数值比较可改变一个应该被检查的元素；协议比较可漏掉终止事件、重复提交或调换两个请求的输出；状态检查可把迟到完成放到槽位复用之后。干预应改变所研究的错误维度，保留其他条件，避免一次同时破坏全部格式而无法知道哪个检查生效。\\\\n\\\\n一个可手工复算的身份反例是：预期集合包含不同请求 A、B，合法输出分别为 17、99。实际轨迹却返回 A=17、B=17。若驱动只保留 A 或将二者错误合并成一个槽，已保留样本的比较可以全部通过，但完整任务不正确。要求 expected、observed 与 terminal 的身份集合在任务定义下对应，同时检查重复、缺失、额外结果和每个身份的内容，才能排除这个假通过。该例是本轮设定的逻辑反例，不代表新运行观测。\\\\n\\\\n空结果集也不能被“全部元素正确”的逻辑真值接受为完成。检查至少要区分应有结果是否齐全、每个结果是否有效、每个状态/终止是否唯一。若协议允许中途取消或部分输出，则其合法预期由取消契约定义，不能随实现返回什么而变化。\\\\n\\\\n## 保留请求、会话和运行的失败范围\\\\n\\\\n一个多轮会话中的后续输入可能依赖前序输出。前一轮失败后，后续未执行属于缺失或被阻断，不能计作验证成功，也不能从预先约定的会话集合中删除。分别报告计划的逻辑轮次、实际发起请求、接纳、拒绝、完成、取消、超时与质量失败；请求指标的分母使用实际发起还是计划请求，必须由任务预先声明，会话成功则需满足该会话的全部必要依赖。请求级条件成功率不能代替整段会话成功率。\\\\n\\\\n检查工具若只记录局部抽样，需声明抽样对象和未覆盖范围。固定 seed 帮助复现特定轨迹，不会自动覆盖所有并发时序；一次完成所有正向样例，也不证明验证器能识别遗漏字段或丢失请求。正向参考与针对性负对照分别提供正确样例和已知错误的辨别证据；选择哪些检查取决于任务与所选机制，不要求每个探索实验复跑全部协议和状态场景。\\\\n\\\\n## 检查缺陷对旧证据的影响\\\\n\\\\n发现检查器遗漏身份、错误比较数值或计时边界错误后，先定位受影响的规则、测试版本和实验，不把所有历史结果笼统清零，也不继续沿用被该缺陷支持的结论。如果原始输出、事件与输入完整，修订后的检查可以重分析这些数据，并保留新旧检查身份；缺少所需信息时必须重跑相应路径。\\\\n\\\\n这是一条证据使用原则，不声称当前运行时会自动发现所有传播关系。设计者应显式说明哪些数值结论、机制判断或系统选择需要复核。检查器修复完成仅恢复了判断能力，不能代替候选通过修订后的检查。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- extracted-character range 0:2979]\\\\n# K-SYS-015：服务主机运行时：执行域、队列与缓冲所有权\\\\n\\\\n推理服务的 CPU 工作包括接收与解析、tokenization、调度、张量准备、提交、结果处理和响应编码。它们有不同的阻塞方式、并行度和生命期，必须与模型算子共享同一份主机资源预算。\\\\n\\\\n## 问题、不变量与设计轴\\\\n\\\\n问题：设备每步只需要主机提交几次工作，但主机还要同时处理连接、分词、调度决策、采样后处理和响应编码；这些工作有的阻塞在 I/O，有的占满一个核，有的必须与设备完成事件同步。要回答的是\\\\\\\"哪些工作放在哪个执行域，域之间用什么通信、容量多大，缓冲属于谁、何时可回收\\\\\\\"。\\\\n\\\\n不变量：每个阶段的队列有界，溢出有明确的拒绝或等待语义；缓冲在同一时刻只有一个写者，跨域传递时所有权转移；取消能到达等待中的任一阶段；主机总 CPU 与内存不超过实际额度（容器 quota、cpuset）；设备提交不被与设备无关的主机工作阻塞。\\\\n\\\\n成本项：跨域通信（锁、队列、IPC 序列化）、上下文切换与缓存污染、每阶段服务时间与并行度的乘积、缓冲驻留（对象大小 × 同时存活数）、以及为了隔离付出的额外进程与复制。\\\\n\\\\n设计轴：执行域划分（单事件循环 / 线程池分阶段 / 多进程 / 混合）；通信方式（共享内存队列 / 管道 / 消息）；队列容量的依据（对象大小与存活范围 / 固定深度 / 按时间）；背压方向（上游拒绝 / 下游丢弃 / 两端协商）；设备提交线程（专用 / 与调度合一）。单进程事件循环加专用提交线程是小 batch 交互服务的常见点；多进程分词与编码在 CPU 占比高时出现。轴上未列点同样合法。\\\\n\\\\n## 何时重新设计执行域\\\\n\\\\n从单请求实现扩展到多请求服务，或观察到设备空闲但请求仍在等待、长输入延迟其他连接、增加 worker 后尾延迟反而上升、取消无法到达等待中的阶段时，主机运行时提供一组可调查的机制。每阶段的工作量与服务时间、真实 CPU/内存额度、原生库线程、设备提交方式和队列占用，可以随原型、profiling 与实验逐步获得，用来区分阻塞、资源争用和通信成本。\\\\n\\\\n执行域划分改变共享状态的更新与协调方式、跨域消息的字节、借用缓冲的生存期以及关闭时的未完工作。顺序执行、锁或原子操作协调的共享状态、消息传递可以形成不同实现，其取舍来自实际争用、搬运和错误传播成本。外部可观察行为见 [服务协议](service-protocol.md)；具体文件和符号位置由当前实现确定。\\\\n\\\\n## 执行域与有界通信\\\\n\\\\n事件循环适合协调大量等待中的连接和完成通知；一个长时间占用该执行域的解析或分词任务会延迟其他连接处理。线程池可以隔离阻塞工作，但是否获得 CPU 并行还取决于运行时和所调用的原生库。进程池增加隔离和独立执行能力，同时引入 IPC、序列化、地址空间和模型副本问题。线程数或进程数本身不是吞吐量。\\\\n\\\\n一个可分析的划分是：网络接入处理请求；输入处理形成带身份的 token/模态张量；调度组织就绪工作；模型执行消费资源；响应处理交付结果。这些是可合并或拆分的责任，既可以在同一调用链完成，也可以跨线程或进程。跨域后，需要解释请求与数据如何对应、谁可更新共享状态以及何时可重用缓冲；具体协调机制随设计变化。\\\\n\\\\n推进方式也可单独选择。由调用方驱动一次工作并消费结果，便于控制观察点；长期执行域接收请求并持续推进，则可能重叠准备、设备执行与结果处理，同时增加排队、通知和在途状态。两种方式都可以支持批处理，也可以混合使用。把同步调用改成返回等待对象，本身没有增加独立工作；收益取决于哪些依赖可以重叠，以及为此增加多少缓冲和协调成本。\\\\n\\\\n任务要求在过载下保持资源有界时，需要约束能够同时进入各阶段的总在途工作。队列容量、上游准入、端到端额度或其他资源管理机制都可以承担这一作用，不必为每条队列设置独立上限。计量单位可以是项数、字节、token 或估计工作量；仅限制请求数会把 100 个短提示与 100 个长视频当作相同负载。若上游生产速率持续高于下游消费速率且没有其他限制，持续积压会增加内存和尾延迟。达到所选预算边界时，可以等待、拒绝或采用任务允许的降载方式，同时保持 deadline 与取消的可达路径。\\\\n\\\\n## 统一计算 CPU 与内存预算\\\\n\\\\n设阶段 j 每请求平均消耗 cⱼ 个 CPU 秒，分配 pⱼ 个有效核，单看该阶段的稳定性必要条件为 λcⱼ<pⱼ。它忽略了方差和排队，因此不足以保证尾延迟。多个阶段共用 CPU 时还要满足总预算，另计模型内部线程、垃圾回收、通信和操作系统工作。\\\\n\\\\n设定 tokenization 每请求占用 8 ms CPU，输入域有两个有效核，其理想上限为 250 请求/秒；事件循环还有每请求 1 ms 的不可重叠 CPU 工作，理想上限为 1000 请求/秒。假设模型可以处理 500 请求/秒，当前输入域已经限制整体。把模型线程翻倍不会消除这个瓶颈；若大量长提示使分词成本翻倍，输入容量还会下降。\\\\n\\\\n主机内存要计入连接缓冲、未分词输入、token 数组、共享 IPC 段、pinned staging 和待发送输出。共享内存省去一次复制，但生产者不能在消费者结束前重用它；进程异常退出后，也需要由明确的资源拥有者回收。复制路径虽然多搬字节，却可能简化生命期并改善隔离，应比较数据大小、频率与错误处理成本。\\\\n\\\\n## 从取消到可回收\\\\n\\\\n| 请求位置 | 取消后的动作 | 仍需保护的对象 |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| 尚在输入队列 | 移除或跳过该代请求 | 仍被其他阶段读取的输入缓冲 |\\\\n| 正在分词或预处理 | 标记结果不再提交，必要时协作停止 | 原生调用在用的输入与输出 |\\\\n| 已提交模型执行 | 禁止后续调度与客户端提交 | 在途 DMA、kernel、通信和 KV |\\\\n| 输出等待发送 | 终止发送，释放已无读者的结果 | 网络层尚未完成的缓冲访问 |\\\\n\\\\n取消标志不能倒转已发起的 DMA，也不能保证一个阻塞调用立即返回。迟到结果携带原请求及代次，不能写进已复用的槽位；最终清理要汇合各执行域的完成事件。对断开连接的响应行为以 [本地 ASGI 规范](../sources/S-ASGI.md) 的相应版本为准，不能把发送函数返回等同于客户端已经消费数据。\\\\n\\\\n## 背压如何连接到模型调度\\\\n\\\\n慢客户端会让输出积累。若每个请求的输出缓冲有上限，服务可以暂停该请求后续生成或按协议终止；暂停又会延长 KV 占用时间。因此网络背压也参与容量准入。批量刷出多个 token 降低封包开销，但增加可见延迟，并改变 ITL 事件位置；不能在没有说明口径时与逐 token 刷出比较。\\\\n\\\\n主机轮询减少唤醒延迟，却占用核和功耗；阻塞等待节省空闲资源，却引入唤醒与调度延迟。完成通知的批处理也存在同样取舍。对延迟敏感的小请求，调度和序列化可能占主导；对大张量，复制与内存带宽可能占主导。两类负载应通过测量决定执行域和缓冲设计。\\\\n\\\\n## 观测与反例\\\\n\\\\n沿同一请求记录各阶段入队、开始、结束、提交和取消事件，区分排队时间与 CPU 服务时间。检查 CPU 实际可用额度、进程/线程数、上下文切换、主存流量和分配次数，避免用“CPU 总\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 4000:7559]\\\\n| 尚未完成输入解释 | 原始字节、媒体大小及待处理工作 | 入口读取、请求准入或输入期限 |\\\\n| 已完成前处理 | token/张量字节、已保留请求数 | 前处理生产者与模型准入 |\\\\n| 已提交的一次执行 | 在途批数、借用输入与暂定状态字节 | 调度器与状态分配器 |\\\\n| 待交付输出 | 内容字节、媒体时长或事件数量 | 响应消费者、后续生成与新准入 |\\\\n| 完成与取消通知 | 尚未处理的控制事件及其责任 | 相应状态拥有者，避免被数据队列永久阻塞 |\\\\n\\\\n有界数据队列也可能阻断终止路径。例如，执行线程必须把结果写入已满队列后才检查取消，而输出线程在等待取消确认时停止取走结果，两者会彼此等待。让等待入队可被取消、由仍可运行的控制路径处理取消，或在排空期间持续消费结果，形成不同解除依赖的方案。独立控制队列或预留通知容量有助于保持消息可达，但仍要保证处理通知的执行域没有被同一个阻塞操作占住。\\\\n\\\\n设定输入队列最多保留 512 个请求，每个原始输入上限 64 KiB，则该层原始字节上限为 32 MiB。若前处理结果还允许另有 512 个、每个最多 4096 个 4 字节 token ID，则该层为 8 MiB；128 个输出队列各保留 64 KiB，又增加 8 MiB。在三类对象能够同时达到上限、且互不共享存储的设定下，这三项合计为 48 MiB，尚未包含 Python/容器元数据、模态张量、IPC、pinned 缓冲与模型状态。\\\\n\\\\n如果处理阶段在生成新表示后立即交还原表示，可以缩短两份对象同时存活的时间；如果只是传递共享内存句柄，同一物理字节不应在物理容量中重复加算，但每个使用者仍有独立生命周期。进程之间复制模型、序列化中间张量或保留调试快照，会产生新的物理副本，应另列。平均请求很小不能证明有界内存，必须用准入允许的输入与同时存活关系计算。\\\\n\\\\n队列上限还会影响延迟。例如固定 worker 服务时间为 5 ms、前面已有 20 个需要串行服务的任务时，忽略其他延迟的等待已为 100 ms；若剩余 deadline 小于此值，继续进入同一队列不会使请求按时完成。真实任务有不同工作量，需按其可估计服务需求与不确定性判断，不能把此设定算例当成所有输入的等待预测。\\\\n\\\\n## 进程输出、超时与关闭也是运行时路径\\\\n\\\\n将预处理或执行放到子进程后，控制消息、结果、stdout/stderr 和进程状态是不同通道。固定 Python subprocess 文档说明，只等待进程结束而不消费有容量限制的输出管道，可能因管道写满形成死锁；一次通信超时也不一定终止子进程。长期 worker 还应避免把无界日志全部缓存在内存中。具体排空方法依赖所用运行时，本章不要求一种统一函数调用。\\\\n\\\\n关闭顺序由对象责任决定：停止新准入，告知拥有者停止未来工作，继续处理能够解除引用的完成事件，最后确认进程与设备相关操作已到达可回收边界。数据队列饱和时，关闭和取消通知仍必须可达。对于无法立即中断的原生调用或设备提交，可以撤销其结果提交资格，再等待完成；将等待超时标成清理成功，会使下一代 worker 继承未知责任。\\\\n\\\\n局部验证检查队列容量、消息归属和重复完成；集成验证在输入、执行、输出分别设置迟到与取消，并加入正在正常运行的邻居请求；系统验证覆盖突发、长短混合、慢消费、日志洪峰和 worker 异常。最终检查各执行域的待办数、实际 CPU 时间、队列字节及共享/私有资源，而不是只用主进程的“活跃请求为零”判定排空。设备上的完成与内存条件参见 [CUDA stream 与分配器](../frameworks/streams-allocator.md)。\\\\n\\\\n<!-- infraagents:provenance -->\\\\n\\\\n## 来源与推导\\\\n\\\\n- [S-ASGI：ASGI — HTTP and WebSocket Message Format](../sources/S-ASGI.md)：ASGI Since these models generate a next token in an au-\\\\ntoregressive manner, one has to run the model multiple times\\\\nto process an inference request where each iteration of the\\\\nmodel generates a single output token for the request. How-\\\\never, existing systems for inference serving do not perform\\\\nwell on this type of workload that has a multi-iteration char-\\\\nacteristic, due to their inﬂexible scheduling mechanism that\\\\ncannot change the current batch of requests being processed;\\\\nrequests that have ﬁnished earlier than other requests in a\\\\nbatch cannot return to the client, while newly arrived requests\\\\nhave to wait until the current batch completely ﬁnishes.\\\\nIn this paper, we propose iteration-level scheduling, a new\\\\nscheduling mechanism that schedules execution at the gran-\\\\nularity of iteration (instead of request) where the scheduler\\\\ninvokes the execution engine to run only a single iteration of\\\\nthe model on the batch. In addition, to apply batching and\\\\niteration-level scheduling to a Transformer model at the same\\\\ntime, we suggest selective batching, which applies batching\\\\nonly to a selected set of operations. Based on these two tech-\\\\nniques, we have implemented a distributed serving system\\\\ncalled ORCA, with additional designs for scalability to models\\\\nwith hundreds of billions of parameters. Our evaluation on a\\\\nGPT-3 175B model shows that ORCA can signiﬁcantly out-\\\\nperform NVIDIA FasterTransformer in terms of both latency\\\\nand throughput: 36.9× throughput improvement at the same\\\\nlevel of latency.\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nLanguage generation tasks are becoming increasingly\\\\nparamount to many types of applications, such as chatbot [9,\\\\n52], summarization [41,45,54], code generation [13], and cap-\\\\ntion generation [65,66]. Moreover, recent works published by\\\\n∗Corresponding author.\\\\nAI21 Labs [37], DeepMind [26,48], Google [15,21,63], Meta\\\\nPlatforms [10,67], Microsoft [50], Microsoft & NVIDIA [59],\\\\nand OpenAI [12] have reported that every language process-\\\\ning task, including translation [11,17], classiﬁcation [20,53],\\\\nquestion-answering [32, 33, 40] and more, can be cast as a\\\\nlanguage generation problem and have shown great improve-\\\\nments along this direction. The rise of generative models is\\\\nnot limited to the language domain; the AI community has\\\\nalso given growing interest to generation problems in other do-\\\\nmains such as image, video, speech, or a mixture of multiple\\\\ndomains [19,38,51,62]. At the heart of generative models lies\\\\nthe Transformer architecture [60] and its variants [15,47–49].\\\\nBy relying on the attention mechanism [60], Transformer\\\\nmodels can learn better representations where each element\\\\nof the sequence may have a direct connection with every other\\\\nelement, which was not possible in recurrent models [25].\\\\nTo use generative models in real-world applications, we\\\\noften delegate the inference procedure to a separate service\\\\nresponsible for ML inference serving. The growing demands\\\\nfor this service, which should provide inference results for\\\\nclient requests at low latency and high throughput, have fa-\\\\ncilitated the development of inference serving systems such\\\\nas Triton Inference Server [7] and TensorFlow Serving [42].\\\\nThese systems can use a separately-developed DNN execution\\\\nengine to perform the actual tensor operations. For example,\\\\nwe can deploy a service for language generation tasks by\\\\nusing a combination of Triton and FasterTransformer [4], an\\\\nexecution engine optimized for the inference of Transformer-\\\\nbased models. In this case, Triton is mainly responsible for\\\\ngrouping multiple client requests into a batch, while Faster-\\\\nTransformer receives the batch from Triton and conducts the\\\\ninference procedure in the batched manner.\\\\nUnfortunately, we notice that the existing inference sys-\\\\ntems, including both the serving system layer and the execu-\\\\ntion engine layer, have limitations in handling requests for\\\\nTransformer-based generative models. Since these models are\\\\ntrained to generate a next token in an autoregressive manner,\\\\none should run the model as many times as the number of to-\\\\nkens to generate, while for other models like ResNet [24] and\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    521\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nBERT [18] a request can be processed by running the model\\\\nonce. That is, in order to process a request to the generative\\\\nmodel, we have to run multiple iterations of the model; each\\\\niteration generates a single output token, which is used as\\\\nan input in the following iteration. Such multi-iteration char-\\\\nacteristic calls into question the current design of inference\\\\nsystems, where the serving system schedules the execution\\\\nof the engine at the granularity of request. Under this design,\\\\nwhen the serving system dispatches a batch of requests to\\\\nthe engine, the engine returns inference results for the entire\\\\nbatch at once after processing all requests within the batch.\\\\nAs different client requests may require different numbers of\\\\niterations for processing, requests that have ﬁnished earlier\\\\nthan others in the batch cannot return to the client, resulting\\\\nin an increased latency. Requests arrived after dispatching the\\\\nbatch also should wait for processing the batch, which can\\\\nsigniﬁcantly increase the requests’ queueing time.\\\\nIn this paper, we propose to schedule the execution of the\\\\nengine at the granularity of iteration instead of request. In\\\\nparticular, the serving system invokes the engine to run only a\\\\nsingle iteration of the model on the batch. As a result, a newly\\\\narrived request can be considered for processing after waiting\\\\nfor only a single iteration of the model. The serving system\\\\nchecks whether a request has ﬁnished processing after every\\\\nreturn from the engine – hence the ﬁnished requests can also\\\\nbe returned to the clients immediately.\\\\nNevertheless, a noticeable challenge arises when we at-\\\\ntempt to apply batching and the iteration-level scheduling at\\\\nthe same time. Unlike the canonical request-level scheduling,\\\\nthe proposed scheduling can issue a batch of requests where\\\\neach request has so far processed a different number of tokens.\\\\nIn such a case, the requests to the Transformer model cannot\\\\nbe processed in the batched manner because the attention\\\\nmechanism calls for non-batchable tensor operations whose\\\\ninput tensors have variable shapes depending on the number\\\\nof processed tokens.\\\\nTo address this challenge, we suggest to apply batching\\\\nonly to a selected set of operations, which we call selective\\\\nbatching. By taking different characteristics of operations into\\\\naccount, selective batching splits the batch and processes each\\\\nrequest individually for the Attention1 operation while apply-\\\\ning batching to other operations of the Transformer model.\\\\nWe observe that the decision not to batch the executions of\\\\nthe Attention operation has only a small impact on efﬁciency.\\\\nSince the Attention operation is not associated with any model\\\\nparameters, applying batching to Attention has no beneﬁt of\\\\nreducing the amount of GPU memory reads by reusing the\\\\nloaded parameters across multiple requests.\\\\nBased on these techniques, we design and implement\\\\nORCA, a distributed serving system for Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models. It takes text as input and produces new text\\\\nas output. Figure 1b shows a Transformer\\\\nlayer used in GPT. Among the operations that compose the\\\\nTransformer layer, Attention is the essence that distinguishes\\\\nTransformer from other architectures. At a high level, the At-\\\\ntention operation computes a weighted average of the tokens\\\\nof interest so that each token in the sequence is aware of the\\\\nother. It takes three inputs, query, key, and value, computes dot\\\\nproducts of the query (for the current token) with all keys (for\\\\nthe tokens of interest), applies Softmax on the dot products\\\\nto get weights, and conducts weighted average of all values\\\\nassociated with the weights.\\\\nSince the Attention requires keys and values of all pre-\\\\nceding tokens,2 we consider the keys and values as internal\\\\nstates that should be maintained across multiple iterations. A\\\\nnaïve, state-less inference procedure would take all tokens in\\\\nthe sequence (including both the client-provided input tokens\\\\nand the output tokens generated so far) to recompute all the\\\\nkeys and values at every iteration. To avoid such recomputa-\\\\ntion, fairseq [43] suggests incremental decoding, which saves\\\\nthe keys and values for reuse in successive iterations. Other\\\\nsystems for Transformer such as FasterTransformer [4] and\\\\nMegatron-LM [3] also do the same.\\\\n2Language models like GPT use causal masking, which means all pre-\\\\nceding tokens are of interest and participate in the Attention operation.\\\\nFigure 1c illustrates the state usage pattern of Transformer,\\\\nalong with LSTM [25] that also maintains internal states. The\\\\nmain difference is that the size of the states (k for Attention\\\\nkey and v for value) in Transformer increases with iteration,\\\\nwhereas the size of the states (c for LSTM internal memory\\\\nand h for LSTM layer’s input/output) in LSTM remains con-\\\\nstant. When processing the token at index t, the Attention\\\\noperation takes all previous Attention keys kl,1:t−1 and values\\\\nvl,1:t−1 along with the current key kl,t and value vl,t.3 There-\\\\nfore, the Attention operation should perform computation on\\\\ntensors of different shapes depending on the number of tokens\\\\nalready processed.\\\\nPrior to the Attention operation, there are the layer normal-\\\\nization operation (LayerNorm) and the QKV Linear (linear\\\\nand split operations to get the query, key and value). Opera-\\\\ntions performed after Attention are, in order, a linear operation\\\\n(Attn Out Linear), an add operation for residual connection\\\\n(Add), layer normalization operation (LayerNorm), the multi-\\\\nlayer perceptron (MLP) operations, and the other residual\\\\nconnection operation (Add).\\\\nML inference serving systems.\\\\nGrowing demands for ML-\\\\ndriven applications have made ML inference serving service\\\\na critical workload in modern datacenters. Users (either the\\\\nend-user or internal microservices of the application) submit\\\\nrequests to an inference service, and the service gives replies\\\\non the requests based on a pre-deﬁned ML model using its\\\\nprovisioned resource, typically equipped with specialized ac-\\\\ncelerators such as GPUs and TPUs. In particular, the service\\\\nruns a DNN model with input data to generate output for the\\\\n3kl,1:t−1 represents Attention keys of the l-th layer for tokens at indices\\\\n1 to t −1 while kl,t is for the Attention key of the l-th layer for the token at\\\\nindex t. Same for vl,1:t−1 and vl,t.\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    523\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 5 ---\\\\nrequest\\\\nresponse\\\\nServing System\\\\nEndpoint\\\\nScheduler\\\\nExecution\\\\nEngine\\\\nRequest Queue\\\\n!\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n#\\\\n$\\\\nx1\\\\nx1: I think\\\\nx2\\\\nx2: I love\\\\nx1\\\\nx1: this is great\\\\nx2\\\\nx2: you\\\\nFigure 2: Overall workﬂow of serving a generative language\\\\nmodel with existing systems.\\\\nrequest. Just like other services operating on datacenters, a\\\\nwell-managed inference service should provide low latency\\\\nand high throughput within a reasonable amount of cost.\\\\nTo meet such constraints, service operators often use ML\\\\ninference serving systems such as Triton Inference Server [7]\\\\nand TensorFlow Serving [42]. These systems can be seen as\\\\nan abstraction sitting atop underlying model execution en-\\\\ngines such as TensorRT [6], TVM [14], TensorFlow [8], and\\\\nmany others [44,46], being agnostic to various kinds of ML\\\\nmodels, execution engines, and computing hardware. While\\\\ndelegating the role of driving the main mathematical opera-\\\\ntions to the engines, serving systems are in charge of exposing\\\\nendpoints that receive inference requests, scheduling execu-\\\\ntions of the engine, and sending responses to the requests.\\\\nAccordingly, these systems focus on aspects such as batch-\\\\ning the executions [7,16,35,42,56], selecting an appropriate\\\\nmodel from multiple model variants [16,27,30,57], deploying\\\\nmultiple models (each for different inference services) on the\\\\nsame device [7,29,35,56], and so on.\\\\nAmong the features and optimizations provided by serv-\\\\ning systems, batching is a key to achieve high accelerator\\\\nutilization when using accelerators like GPUs. When we run\\\\nthe execution engine with batching enabled, the input tensors\\\\nfrom multiple requests coalesce into a single, large input ten-\\\\nsor before being fed to the ﬁrst operation of the model. Since\\\\nthe accelerators prefer large input tensors over small ones to\\\\nbetter exploit the vast amount of parallel computation units,\\\\nthe engine’s throughput is highly dependent on the batch size,\\\\ni.e., the number of inference requests the engine processes\\\\ntogether. Reusing the model parameters loaded from off-chip\\\\nmemory is another merit in batched execution, especially\\\\nwhen the model involves memory-intensive operations.\\\\nFigure 2 shows an overall workﬂow of serving a generative\\\\nlanguage model with existing serving systems and execution\\\\nengines. The main component of the serving system (e.g., Tri-\\\\nton [7]) is the scheduler, which is responsible for  creating\\\\na batch of requests by retrieving requests from a queue and \\\\nscheduling the execution engine (e.g., FasterTransformer [4])\\\\nto process the batch. The execution engine  processes the\\\\nreceived batch by running multiple iterations of the model\\\\nbeing served and  returns the generated text back to the\\\\nserving system. In Figure 2, the serving system schedules the\\\\nengine to process two requests (x1: “I think”, x2: “I love”) in\\\\niter 1\\\\nx1\\\\nx1\\\\nx2\\\\nx2\\\\niter 2\\\\nI\\\\nthink\\\\nI\\\\nlove\\\\nthis\\\\nyou\\\\nthis\\\\nyou\\\\niter 3\\\\nis\\\\n-\\\\nis\\\\n<EOS>\\\\ngreat\\\\n-\\\\niter 4\\\\ngreat\\\\n-\\\\n<EOS>\\\\n-\\\\nFigure 3: An illustration for a case where the requests have the\\\\nsame input length but some requests ﬁnish earlier than others.\\\\nShaded tokens represent input tokens. “-” denotes inputs and\\\\noutputs of extra computation imposed by the scheduling.\\\\na batch and the engine generates “this is great” and “you” for\\\\nrequests x1 and x2, respectively.\\\\n3\\\\nChallenges and Proposed Solutions\\\\nIn this section, we describe challenges in serving Transformer-\\\\nbased generative models and propose two techniques:\\\\niteration-level scheduling and selective batching.\\\\nC1: Early-ﬁnished and late-joining requests.\\\\nOne major\\\\nlimitation of existing systems is that the serving system and\\\\nthe execution engine interact with each other only when (1)\\\\nthe serving system schedules the next batch on an idle engine;\\\\nor (2) the engine ﬁnishes processing the current batch. In\\\\nother words, these systems are designed to schedule execu-\\\\ntions at request granularity; the engine maintains a batch of\\\\nrequests ﬁxed until all requests in the batch ﬁnish. This can be\\\\nproblematic in the serving of generative models, since each\\\\nrequest in a batch may require different number of iterations,\\\\nresulting in certain requests ﬁnishing earlier than the others.\\\\nIn the example shown in Figure 3, although request x2 ﬁnishes\\\\nearlier than request x1, the engine performs computation for\\\\nboth “active” and “inactive” requests throughout all iterations.\\\\nSuch extra computation for inactive requests (x2 at iter 3 and\\\\n4) limits the efﬁciency of batched execution.\\\\nWhat makes it even worse is that this behavior prevents an\\\\nearly return of the ﬁnished request to the client, imposing a\\\\nsubstantial amount of extra latency. This is because the engine\\\\nonly returns the execution results to the serving system when\\\\nit ﬁnishes processing all requests in the batch. Similarly, when\\\\na new request arrives in the middle of the current batch’s\\\\nexecution, the aforementioned scheduling mechanism makes\\\\nthe newly arrived request wait until all requests in the current\\\\nbatch have ﬁnished. We argue that the current request-level\\\\nscheduling mechanism cannot efﬁciently handle workloads\\\\nwith multi-iteration characteristic. Note that this problem of\\\\nearly-ﬁnished and late-joining requests does not occur in the\\\\ntraining of language models; the training procedure ﬁnishes\\\\nprocessing the whole batch in a single iteration by using the\\\\nteacher forcing technique [64].\\\\n524    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\nresponse\\\\nOrca System\\\\nEndpoint\\\\nrequest\\\\nScheduler\\\\nRequest Pool\\\\nExecution\\\\nEngine\\\\n!\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n#\\\\nx1\\\\nx1 x11\\\\nx11 x12\\\\nx12 x13\\\\nx13 x14\\\\nx14\\\\nx2\\\\nx2 x21\\\\nx21 x22\\\\nx22\\\\nx3\\\\nx3 x31\\\\nx31 x32\\\\nx32\\\\nx4\\\\nx4 x41\\\\nx41 x42\\\\nx42 x43\\\\nx43\\\\nx1, x2, x3, x4\\\\nx1, x2, x3, x4\\\\n· · ·\\\\n· · ·\\\\nx15, x23, x33, x44\\\\nx15, x23, x33, x44\\\\n$\\\\nFigure 4: System overview of ORCA. Interactions between\\\\ncomponents represented as dotted lines indicate that the inter-\\\\naction takes place at every iteration of the execution engine.\\\\nxi j is the j-th token of the i-th request. Shaded tokens repre-\\\\nsent input tokens received from the clients, while unshaded\\\\ntokens are generated by ORCA. For example, request x1 ini-\\\\ntially arrived with two input tokens (x11,x12) and have run\\\\ntwo iterations so far, where the ﬁrst and second iterations gen-\\\\nerated x13 and x14, respectively. On the other hand, request\\\\nx3 only contains input tokens (x31,x32) because it has not run\\\\nany iterations yet.\\\\nS1: Iteration-level scheduling.\\\\nTo address the above limi-\\\\ntations, we propose to schedule executions at the granularity\\\\nof iteration. At high level, the scheduler repeats the follow-\\\\ning procedure: (1) selects requests to run next; (2) invokes\\\\nthe engine to execute one iteration for the selected requests;\\\\nand (3) receives execution results for the scheduled iteration.\\\\nSince the scheduler receives a return on every iteration, it can\\\\ndetect the completion of a request and immediately return its\\\\ngenerated tokens to the client. For a newly arrived request, the\\\\nrequest gets a chance to start processing (i.e., the scheduler\\\\nmay select the new request to run next) after execution of\\\\nthe currently scheduled iteration, signiﬁcantly reducing the\\\\nqueueing delay. With iteration-level scheduling, the sched-\\\\nuler has a full control on how many and which requests are\\\\nprocessed in each iteration.\\\\nFigure 4 depicts the system architecture and the overall\\\\nworkﬂow of ORCA using the iteration-level scheduling. ORCA\\\\nexposes an endpoint (e.g., HTTPS or gRPC) where inference\\\\nrequests arrive at the system and responses to the requests\\\\nare sent out. The endpoint puts newly arrived requests in the\\\\nrequest pool, a component that manages all requests in the\\\\nsystem during their lifetime. The pool is monitored by the\\\\nscheduler, which is responsible for: selecting a set of requests\\\\nfrom the pool, scheduling the execution engine to run an it-\\\\neration of the model on the set, receiving execution results\\\\n(i.e., output tokens) from the engine, and updating the pool\\\\nby appending each output token to the corresponding request.\\\\nThe engine is an abstraction for executing the actual tensor\\\\noperations, which can be parallelized across multiple GPUs\\\\nspread across multiple machines. In the example shown in\\\\nFigure 4, the scheduler  interacts with the request pool to\\\\ndecide which requests to run next and  invokes the engine\\\\nto run four selected requests: (x1,x2,x3,x4). The scheduler\\\\nprovides the engine with input tokens of the requests sched-\\\\nuled for the ﬁrst time. In this case, x3 and x4 have not run\\\\nany iterations yet, so the scheduler hands over (x31,x32) for\\\\nx3 and (x41,x42,x43) for x4. The engine  runs an iteration\\\\nof the model on the four requests and  returns generated\\\\noutput tokens (x15,x23,x33,x44), one for each scheduled re-\\\\nquest. Once a request has ﬁnished processing, the request pool\\\\nremoves the ﬁnished request and notiﬁes the endpoint to send\\\\na response. Unlike the method shown in Figure 2 that should\\\\nrun multiple iterations on a scheduled batch until ﬁnish of\\\\nall requests within the batch, ORCA’s scheduler can change\\\\nwhich requests are going to be processed at every iteration.\\\\nWe describe the detailed algorithm about how to select the\\\\nrequests at every iteration in Section 4.2.\\\\nC2: Batching an arbitrary set of requests.\\\\nWhen we try\\\\nto use the iteration-level scheduling in practice, one major\\\\nchallenge that we are going to face is batching. To achieve\\\\nhigh efﬁciency, the execution engine should be able to process\\\\nany selected set of requests in the batched manner. Without\\\\nbatching, one would have to process each selected request\\\\none by one, losing out on the massively parallel computation\\\\ncapabilities of GPUs.\\\\nUnfortunately, there is no guarantee that even for a pair of\\\\nrequests (xi,xj), for the next iteration, their executions can be\\\\nmerged and replaced with a batched version. There are three\\\\ncases for a pair of requests where the next iteration cannot\\\\nbe batched together: (1) both requests are in the initiation\\\\nphase and each has different number of input tokens (e.g.,\\\\nx3 and x4 in Figure 4); (2) both are in the increment phase\\\\nand each is processing a token at different index from each\\\\nother (x1 and x2); or (3) each request is in the different phase:\\\\ninitiation or increment (x1 and x3). Recall that in order to\\\\nbatch the execution of multiple requests, the execution of each\\\\nrequest must consist of identical operations, each consuming\\\\nidentically-shaped input tensors. In the ﬁrst case, the two\\\\nrequests cannot be processed in a batch because the “length”\\\\ndimension of their input tensors, which is the number of input\\\\ntokens, are not equal. The requests in the second case have\\\\ndifference in the tensor shape of Attention keys and values\\\\nbecause each processes token at different index, as shown in\\\\nFigure 1c. For the third case, we cannot batch the iterations of\\\\ndifferent phases because they take different number of tokens\\\\nas input; an iteration of the initiation phase processes all input\\\\ntokens in parallel for efﬁciency, while in the increment phase\\\\neach iteration takes a single token as its input (we assume the\\\\nuse of fairseq-style incremental decoding [43]).\\\\nBatching is only applicable when the two selected requests\\\\nare in the same phase, with the same number of input tokens\\\\n(in case of the initiation phase) or with the same token index\\\\n(in case of the increment phase). This restriction signiﬁcantly\\\\nreduces the likelihood of batching in real-world workloads,\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    525\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\nQKV Linear\\\\nSplit\\\\nAttention K/V Manager\\\\nAttn x4\\\\nx4\\\\nAttn x3\\\\nx3\\\\nAttn x2\\\\nx2\\\\nAttn x1\\\\nx1\\\\nLayer Input\\\\nKey\\\\nValue\\\\nx1 : (x11, x12, x13)\\\\nx1 : (x11, x12, x13)\\\\nx2 : (x21)\\\\nx2 : (x21)\\\\nMerge\\\\nAttn Out \\\\nLinear\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n· · ·\\\\n· · ·\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[2, 3H]\\\\n[2, 3H]\\\\n[3, 3H]\\\\n[3, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[7, 3H]\\\\n[7, 3H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\nx32\\\\nx32\\\\nx41\\\\nx41 x42\\\\nx42 x43\\\\nx43\\\\nx14\\\\nx14\\\\nx22\\\\nx22\\\\nx31\\\\nx31\\\\n[2, H]\\\\n[2, H]\\\\n[3, H]\\\\n[3, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\nFigure 5: An illustration of ORCA execution engine running\\\\na Transformer layer on a batch of requests with selective\\\\nbatching. We only depict the QKV Linear, Attention, and\\\\nAttention Out Linear operations for simplicity.\\\\nbecause the scheduler should make a wish for the presence\\\\nof two requests eligible for batching at the same time. The\\\\nlikelihood further decreases exponentially as the batch size\\\\nincreases, making it impractical to use a large batch size that\\\\ncan pull out better throughput without compromising latency.\\\\nS2: Selective batching.\\\\nWe propose selective batching, a\\\\ntechnique for batched execution that allows high ﬂexibility in\\\\ncomposing requests as a batch. Instead of processing a batch\\\\nof requests by “batchifying” all tensor operations composing\\\\nthe model, this technique selectively apply batching only to a\\\\nhandful of operations.\\\\nThe main problem regarding batching described above is\\\\nthat the three aforementioned cases4 correspond to irregu-\\\\nlarly shaped input (or state) tensors, which cannot be coa-\\\\nlesced into a single large tensor and fed into a batch opera-\\\\ntion. In the canonical batching mechanism, at each iteration,\\\\na Transformer layer takes a 3-dimensional input tensor of\\\\nshape [B,L,H] generated by concatenating multiple [L,H] in-\\\\nput tensors of requests in a batch, where B is the batch size,\\\\nL is the number of tokens processed together, and H is the\\\\nhidden size of the model. For example, in Figure 3, “iter 1”\\\\n(initiation phase) takes an input tensor of shape [2,2,H] and\\\\n“iter 2” (increment phase) takes a tensor of shape [2,1,H].\\\\nHowever, when the scheduler decides to run an iteration on\\\\nbatch (x1,x2,x3,x4) in Figure 4, the inputs for requests in the\\\\ninitiation phase (x3 : [2,H] and x4 : [3,H]) cannot coalesce\\\\ninto a single tensor of shape [B,L,H] because x3 and x4 have\\\\ndifferent number of input tokens, 2 and 3.\\\\nInterestingly, not all operations are incompatible with such\\\\nirregularly shaped tensors. Operations such as non-Attention\\\\nmatrix multiplication and layer normalization can be made to\\\\nwork with irregularly shaped tensors by ﬂattening the tensors.\\\\n4We use the ﬁrst case as a driving example, but the argument can be\\\\nsimilarly applied to the other two cases.\\\\nFor instance, the aforementioned input tensors for x3 and x4\\\\ncan compose a 2-dimensional tensor of shape [∑L,H] = [5,H]\\\\nwithout an explicit batch dimension. This tensor can be fed\\\\ninto all non-Attention operations including Linear, Layer-\\\\nNorm, Add, and GeLU operations because they do not need to\\\\ndistinguish tensor elements of different requests. On the other\\\\nhand, the Attention operation requires a notion of requests\\\\n(i.e., requires the batch dimension) to compute attention only\\\\nbetween the tokens of the same request, typically done by\\\\napplying cuBLAS routines for batch matrix multiplication.\\\\nSelective batching is aware of the different characteristics\\\\nof each operation; it splits the batch and processes each re-\\\\nquest individually for the Attention operation while applying\\\\ntoken-wise (instead of request-wise) batching to other oper-\\\\nations without the notion of requests. Figure 5 presents the\\\\nselective batching mechanism processing a batch of requests\\\\n(x1,x2,x3,x4) described in Figure 4. This batch has 7 input\\\\ntokens to process, so we make the input tensor have a shape\\\\nof [7,H] and apply the non-Attention operations. Before the\\\\nAttention operation, we insert a Split operation and run the\\\\nAttention operation separately on the split tensor for each\\\\nrequest. The outputs of Attention operations are merged back\\\\ninto a tensor of shape [7,H] by a Merge operation, bringing\\\\nback the batching functionality to the rest of operations.\\\\nTo make the requests in the increment phase can use the\\\\nAttention keys and values for the tokens processed in previous\\\\niterations, ORCA maintains the generated keys and values in\\\\nthe Attention K/V manager. The manager maintains these\\\\nkeys and values separately for each request until the scheduler\\\\nexplicitly asks to remove certain request’s keys and values,\\\\ni.e., when the request has ﬁnished processing. The Attention\\\\noperation for request in the increment phase (x1 and x2) takes\\\\nkeys and values of previous tokens (x11,x12,x13 for x1; x21 for\\\\nx2) from the manager, along with the current token’s query,\\\\nkey, and value from the Split operation to compute attention\\\\nbetween the current token and the previous ones.\\\\n4\\\\nORCA Design\\\\nBased on the above techniques, we design and implement\\\\nORCA: a distributed serving system for Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models. We have already discussed the system\\\\ncomponents and the overall execution model of ORCA while\\\\ndescribing Figure 4. In this section, we answer the remaining\\\\nissues about how to build an efﬁcient system that can scale to\\\\nlarge-scale models with hundreds of billions of parameters.\\\\nWe also describe the scheduling algorithm for iteration-level\\\\nscheduling, i.e., how to select a batch of requests from the\\\\nrequest pool at every iteration.\\\\n4.1\\\\nDistributed Architecture\\\\nRecent works [12,31] have shown that scaling language mod-\\\\nels can dramatically improve the quality of models. Hence,\\\\n526    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 8 ---\\\\nLayer1\\\\nLayer2\\\\nLayer3\\\\nLayer4\\\\nGPU1\\\\nGPU2\\\\nGPU3\\\\nGPU4\\\\nGPU5\\\\nGPU6\\\\nFigure 6: An example of intra- and inter- layer parallelism. A\\\\nvertical dotted line indicates partitioning between layers and\\\\na horizontal line indicates partitioning within a layer.\\\\nExecution Engine\\\\nScheduler\\\\nController\\\\nControl Plane\\\\nData Plane\\\\nWorker 1\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nEngine Master\\\\nschedule\\\\ntokens\\\\nController\\\\nWorker 2\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\ntokens\\\\ncontrol\\\\nmessage\\\\ncontrol\\\\nmessage\\\\ntokens\\\\nFigure 7: An illustration of the distributed architecture of\\\\nORCA’s execution engine using the parallelization conﬁgura-\\\\ntion shown in Figure 6. For example, the ﬁrst inter-layer parti-\\\\ntion (Layer1 and Layer2) in Figure 6 is assigned to Worker1,\\\\nwhile the second partition is assigned to Worker2.\\\\nsystem support for serving such large language models is get-\\\\nting more importance, especially when the model does not ﬁt\\\\nin a single GPU. In such a case, one should split the model\\\\nparameters along with the corresponding computation and\\\\ndistribute them across multiple GPUs and machines.\\\\nORCA composes known parallelization techniques for\\\\nTransformer models: intra-layer parallelism and inter-layer\\\\nparallelism. These two model parallelism strategies, which\\\\nare also used by FasterTransformer [4], have been origi-\\\\nnally developed for distributed training. Intra-layer paral-\\\\nlelism [55,58] splits matrix multiplications (i.e., Linear and\\\\nAttention operations) and their associated parameters over\\\\nmultiple GPUs. We omit the detail about how this strat-\\\\negy partitions each matrix multiplication. On the other hand,\\\\ninter-layer parallelism splits Transformer layers over multiple\\\\nGPUs. ORCA assigns the same number of Transformer layers\\\\nto each GPU. Figure 6 illustrates an example application of\\\\nintra- and inter- layer parallelism to a 4-layer GPT model. The\\\\n4 layers are split into 2 inter-layer partitions, and the layers in\\\\nthe partition are subdivided into 3 intra-layer partitions. We\\\\nassign each partition to a GPU, using a total of 6 GPUs.\\\\nThe ORCA execution engine supports distributed execution\\\\nusing the techniques described above. Figure 7 depicts the\\\\narchitecture of an ORCA engine. Each worker process is re-\\\\nsponsible for an inter-layer partition of the model and can be\\\\nplaced on a different machine from each other. In particular,\\\\neach worker manages one or more CPU threads each dedi-\\\\ncated for controlling a GPU, the number of which depends on\\\\nthe degree of intra-layer parallelism.\\\\nThe execution procedure of the ORCA execution engine is\\\\nas follows. Once the engine is scheduled to run an iteration of\\\\nthe model for a batch of requests, the engine master forwards\\\\nthe received information about the scheduled batch to the ﬁrst\\\\nworker process (Worker1). The information includes tokens\\\\nfor the current iteration and a control message, which is com-\\\\nposed of ids of requests within the batch, current token index\\\\n(for requests in the increment phase), and number of input\\\\ntokens (for requests in the initiation phase). The controller of\\\\nWorker1 hands over the information received from the engine\\\\nmaster to the GPU-controlling threads, where each thread\\\\nparses the information and issues proper GPU kernels to its\\\\nassociated GPU. For example, the kernel for the Attention\\\\noperation uses the request id and the current token index to get\\\\nthe GPU memory address of previous keys and values kept by\\\\nthe Attention K/V manager. In the meantime, the controller\\\\nalso forwards the control message to the controller of the next\\\\nworker (Worker2), without waiting for the completion of the\\\\nkernels issued on the GPUs of Worker1. Unlike Worker1, the\\\\ncontroller of the last worker (Worker2) waits for (i.e., syn-\\\\nchronize with) the completion of the issued GPU kernels, in\\\\norder to fetch the output token for each request and send the\\\\ntokens back to the engine master.\\\\nTo keep GPUs busy as much as possible, we design the\\\\nORCA engine to minimize synchronization between the CPU\\\\nand GPUs. We observe that current systems for distributed\\\\ninference (e.g., FasterTransformer [4] and Megatron-LM [3])\\\\nhave CPU-GPU synchronization whenever each process re-\\\\nceives control messages5 because they exchange the messages\\\\nthrough a GPU-to-GPU communication channel – NCCL [5].\\\\nThe exchange of these control messages occurs at every iter-\\\\nation, imposing a non-negligible performance overhead. On\\\\nthe other hand, ORCA separates the communication channels\\\\nfor control messages (plus tokens) and tensor data transfer,\\\\navoiding the use of NCCL for data used by CPUs. Figure 7\\\\nshows that the ORCA engine uses NCCL exclusively for ex-\\\\nchanging intermediate tensor data (represented by dashed\\\\narrows) as this data is produced and consumed by GPUs. Con-\\\\ntrol messages, which is used by the CPU threads for issuing\\\\nGPU kernels, sent between the engine master and worker con-\\\\ntrollers by a separate communication channel that does not\\\\ninvolve GPU such as gRPC [2].\\\\n4.2\\\\nScheduling Algorithm\\\\nThe ORCA scheduler makes decisions on which requests\\\\nshould be selected and processed at every iteration. The sched-\\\\nuler has high ﬂexibility in selecting a set of requests to com-\\\\n5This includes various metadata such as batch size, sequence length, and\\\\nwhether a request within the batch has ﬁnished processing.\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    527\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 9 ---\\\\npose a batch, because of the selective batching technique that\\\\nallows the engine to run any set of requests in the batched\\\\nmanner. Now the main question left is how to select the re-\\\\nquests at every iteration.\\\\nWe design the ORCA scheduler to use a simple algorithm\\\\nthat does not change the processing order of client requests;\\\\nearly-arrived requests are processed earlier. That is, we en-\\\\nsure iteration-level ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-served (FCFS) property.\\\\nWe deﬁne the iteration-level FCFS property for workloads\\\\nwith multi-iteration characteristics as follows: for any pair\\\\nof requests (xi,xj) in the request pool, if xi has arrived ear-\\\\nlier than x j, xi should have run the same or more iterations\\\\nthan xj. Note that some late-arrived requests may return ear-\\\\nlier to clients if the late request requires a smaller number of\\\\niterations to ﬁnish.\\\\nStill, the scheduler needs to take into account additional\\\\nfactors: diminishing returns to increasing the batch size and\\\\nGPU memory constraint. Increasing the batch size trades off\\\\nincreased throughput for increased latency, but as the batch\\\\nsize becomes larger, the amount of return (i.e., increase in\\\\nthroughput) diminishes. Therefore, just like other serving sys-\\\\ntems [7,16], ORCA also has a notion of a max batch size: the\\\\nlargest possible number of requests within a batch. The ORCA\\\\nsystem operator can tune this knob to maximize throughput\\\\nwhile satisfying one’s latency budget. We will discuss this in\\\\nmore details with experiment results in Section 6.2.\\\\nAnother factor is the GPU memory constraint. Optimiz-\\\\ning memory usage by reusing buffers for intermediate results\\\\nacross multiple operations is a well-known technique used by\\\\nvarious systems [4,6], and ORCA also adopts this technique.\\\\nHowever, unlike the buffers for intermediate results that can\\\\nbe reused immediately, buffers used by the Attention K/V\\\\nmanager for storing the keys and values cannot be reclaimed\\\\nuntil the ORCA scheduler notiﬁes that the corresponding re-\\\\nquest has ﬁnished processing. A naïve implementation can\\\\nmake the scheduler fall into a deadlock when the scheduler\\\\ncannot issue an iteration for any requests in the pool because\\\\nthere is no space left for storing a new Attention key and value\\\\nfor the next token. This requires the ORCA scheduler to be\\\\naware of the remaining size of pre-allocated memory regions\\\\nfor the manager.\\\\nThe ORCA scheduler takes all these factors into account:\\\\nit selects at most “max batch size” requests based on the ar-\\\\nrival time, while reserving enough space for storing keys and\\\\nvalues to a request when the request is scheduled for the ﬁrst\\\\ntime. We describe the scheduling process in Algorithm 1. The\\\\nalgorithm selects a batch of requests from the request pool\\\\n(line 4) and schedules the batch (line 5). The Select function\\\\n(line 17) selects at most max_bs requests from the pool based\\\\non the arrival time of the request (lines 20-22). Algorithm 1\\\\ndoes not depict the procedure of request arrival and return;\\\\none may think of it as there exist concurrent threads insert-\\\\ning newly arrived requests into request_pool and removing\\\\nﬁnished requests from request_pool.\\\\nAlgorithm 1: ORCA scheduling algorithm\\\\nParams: n_workers: number of workers, max_bs:\\\\nmax batch size, n_slots: number of K/V slots\\\\n1 n_scheduled ←0\\\\n2 n_rsrv ←0\\\\n3 while true do\\\\n4\\\\nbatch,n_rsrv ←Select(request_pool,n_rsrv)\\\\n5\\\\nschedule engine to run one iteration of\\\\nthe model for the batch\\\\n6\\\\nforeach req in batch do\\\\n7\\\\nreq.state ←RUNNING\\\\n8\\\\nn_scheduled ←n_scheduled +1\\\\n9\\\\nif n_scheduled = n_workers then\\\\n10\\\\nwait for return of a scheduled batch\\\\n11\\\\nforeach req in the returned batch do\\\\n12\\\\nreq.state ←INCREMENT\\\\n13\\\\nif ﬁnished(req) then\\\\n14\\\\nn_rsrv ←n_rsrv−req.max_tokens\\\\n15\\\\nn_scheduled ←n_scheduled −1\\\\n16\\\\n17 def Select(pool, n_rsrv):\\\\n18\\\\nbatch ←{}\\\\n19\\\\npool ←{req ∈pool|req.state ̸= RUNNING}\\\\n20\\\\nSortByArrivalTime(pool)\\\\n21\\\\nforeach req in pool do\\\\n22\\\\nif batch.size() = max_bs then break\\\\n23\\\\nif req.state = INITIATION then\\\\n24\\\\nnew_n_rsrv ←n_rsrv+req.max_tokens\\\\n25\\\\nif new_n_rsrv > n_slots then break\\\\n26\\\\nn_rsrv ←new_n_rsrv\\\\n27\\\\nbatch ←batchS{req}\\\\n28\\\\nreturn batch,n_rsrv\\\\nWhen the scheduler considers a request in the initiation\\\\nphase, meaning that the request has never been scheduled\\\\nyet, the scheduler uses the request’s max_tokens6 attribute\\\\nto reserve max_tokens slots of GPU memory for storing the\\\\nkeys and values in advance (lines 23-26). The scheduler deter-\\\\nmines whether the reservation is possible (line 25) based on\\\\nn_rsrv, the number of currently reserved slots, where a slot\\\\nis deﬁned by the amount of memory required for storing an\\\\nAttention key and value for a single token. Here, n_slots is a\\\\nparameter tuned by the ORCA system operator indicating the\\\\nsize of memory region (in terms of slots) allocated to the At-\\\\ntention K/V manager. Since the number of tokens in a request\\\\ncannot exceed max_tokens, if the reservation is possible, it\\\\nis guaranteed that the manager can allocate buffers for the\\\\nnewly generated keys and values until the request ﬁnishes.\\\\nUnlike the tuning of max_bs that requires quantifying the\\\\ntrade-off between latency and throughput, the ORCA system\\\\n6The max_tokens attribute is a per-request option, meaning the maximum\\\\nnumber of tokens that a request can have after processing.\\\\n528    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 10 ---\\\\nWorker1\\\\nWorker2\\\\nWorker3\\\\nTime\\\\nA1B1\\\\nA1B1\\\\nA1B1\\\\nC1D1\\\\nC1D1\\\\nC1D1\\\\nE1F1\\\\nE1F1\\\\nE1F1\\\\nA2B2\\\\nA2B2\\\\nA2B2\\\\nC2D2\\\\nC2D2\\\\nE2F2\\\\n(a) ORCA execution pipeline.\\\\nPartition1\\\\nPartition2\\\\nPartition3\\\\nA1\\\\nTime\\\\nB1\\\\nA1\\\\nB1\\\\nA1\\\\nB1\\\\nA2\\\\nB2\\\\nA2\\\\nB2\\\\nA2\\\\nB2\\\\nA3\\\\n(b) FasterTransformer execution pipeline.\\\\nFigure 8: Comparison of the use of pipeline parallelism in\\\\nORCA and FasterTransformer where Xi is the i-th iteration of\\\\nrequest X.\\\\noperator can easily conﬁgure n_slots without any experiments.\\\\nGiven a model speciﬁcation (e.g., hidden size, number of\\\\nlayers, etc.) and degrees of intra- and inter- layer parallelism,\\\\nORCA’s GPU memory usage mostly depends on n_slots. That\\\\nis, the operator can simply use the largest possible n_slots\\\\nunder the memory constraint.\\\\nPipeline parallelism.\\\\nORCA’s scheduler makes the execu-\\\\ntion of workers in the engine to be pipelined across multi-\\\\nple batches. The scheduler does not wait for the return of a\\\\nscheduled batch until n_scheduled, the number of currently\\\\nscheduled batches, reaches n_workers (line 9-10 of Algo-\\\\nrithm 1). By doing so, the scheduler keeps the number of\\\\nconcurrently running batches in the engine to be n_workers,\\\\nwhich means that every worker in the engine is processing\\\\none of the batches without being idle.\\\\nFigure 8a depicts the execution pipeline of 3 ORCA work-\\\\ners, using a max batch size of 2. We assume that the request\\\\nA arrives before B, which arrives before C, and so on. At ﬁrst,\\\\nthe scheduler selects requests A and B based on the arrival\\\\ntime and schedules the engine to process a batch of requests\\\\nA and B (we call this batch AB), where Worker1, Worker2,\\\\nand Worker3 process the batch in turn. The scheduler waits\\\\nfor the return of the batch AB only after the scheduler injects\\\\ntwo more batches: CD and EF. Once the batch AB returns,\\\\nrequests A and B get selected and scheduled once again, be-\\\\ncause they are the earliest arrived requests among the requests\\\\nin the pool.\\\\nIn contrast, the interface between current serving systems\\\\nand execution engines (e.g., a combination of Triton [7]\\\\nand FasterTransformer [4]) does not allow injecting another\\\\nbatch before the ﬁnish of the current running batch, due to\\\\nthe request-level scheduling. That is, Triton cannot inject\\\\nthe next request C to FasterTransformer until the current\\\\n# Params\\\\n# Layers\\\\nHidden\\\\nsize\\\\n# Inter-\\\\npartitions\\\\n# Intra-\\\\npartitions\\\\n13B\\\\n40\\\\n5120\\\\n1\\\\n1\\\\n101B\\\\n80\\\\n10240\\\\n1\\\\n8\\\\n175B\\\\n96\\\\n12288\\\\n2\\\\n8\\\\n341B\\\\n120\\\\n15360\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nTable 1: Conﬁgurations of models used in the experiments.\\\\nbatch AB ﬁnishes. To enable pipelined execution of multiple\\\\ninter-layer partitions under such constraint, FasterTransformer\\\\nsplits a batch of requests into multiple microbatches [28] and\\\\npipelines the executions of partitions across the microbatches.\\\\nIn Figure 8b, FasterTransformer splits the batch AB into two\\\\nmicrobatches, A and B. Since each partition processes a mi-\\\\ncrobatch (which is smaller than the original batch) in the\\\\nbatched manner, the performance gain from batching can\\\\nbecome smaller. Moreover, this method may insert bubbles\\\\ninto the pipeline when the microbatch size is too large, mak-\\\\ning the number of microbatches smaller than the number of\\\\npartitions. While FasterTransformer needs to trade batching\\\\nefﬁciency (larger microbatch size) for pipelining efﬁciency\\\\n(fewer pipeline bubbles), ORCA is free of such a tradeoff –\\\\nthanks to iteration-level scheduling – and can easily pipeline\\\\nrequests without dividing a batch into microbatches.\\\\n5\\\\nImplementation\\\\nWe have implemented ORCA with 13K lines of C++, based\\\\non the CUDA ecosystem. We use gRPC [2] for the com-\\\\nmunication in the control plane of the ORCA engine, while\\\\nNCCL [5] is used in the data plane, for both inter-layer and\\\\nintra-layer communication. Since we design ORCA to fo-\\\\ncus on Transformer-based generative models, ORCA pro-\\\\nvides popular Transformer layers as a building block of mod-\\\\nels including the original encoder-decoder Transformer [60],\\\\nGPT [47], and other variants discussed in Raffel et al. [49].\\\\nWe have also implemented fused kernels for LayerNorm,\\\\nAttention, and GeLU operators, just like other systems for\\\\ntraining or inference of Transformer models [1, 4, 58]. For\\\\nexample, the procedure of computing dot products between\\\\nAttention query and keys, Softmax on the dot products, and\\\\nweighted average of Attention values are fused into a single\\\\nCUDA kernel for the Attention operator. In addition, we go\\\\none step further and fuse the kernels of the split Attention\\\\noperators by simply concatenating all thread blocks of the\\\\nkernels for different requests. Although this fusion makes the\\\\nthread blocks within a kernel have different characteristics and\\\\nlifetimes (which is often discouraged by CUDA programming\\\\npractice) because they process tensors of different shapes, we\\\\nﬁnd this fusion to be beneﬁcial by improving GPU utilization\\\\nand reducing the kernel launch overhead [34,39].\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    529\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 11 ---\\\\n6\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nIn this section, we present evaluation results to show the\\\\nefﬁciency of ORCA.\\\\nEnvironment.\\\\nWe run our evaluation on Azure ND96asr\\\\nA100 v4 VMs, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA 40-GB A100\\\\nGPUs connected over NVLink. We use at most four VMs\\\\ndepending on the size of the model being tested. Each VM\\\\nhas 8 Mellanox 200Gbps HDR Inﬁniband adapters, providing\\\\nan 1.6Tb/s of interconnect bandwidth between VMs.\\\\nModels.\\\\nThroughout the experiments, we use GPT [12] as a\\\\nrepresentative example of Transformer-based generative mod-\\\\nels. Based on these two mod-\\\\nels, we change the number of layers and hidden size to make\\\\nconﬁgurations for 101B and 341B models. While there exist other\\\\nsystems with the support for distributed execution such as\\\\nMegatron-LM [3] and DeepSpeed [1], these systems are pri-\\\\nmarily designed and optimized for training workloads, which\\\\nmakes them show relatively lower performance compared to\\\\nthe inference-optimized systems.\\\\nScenarios.\\\\nWe use two different scenarios to drive our eval-\\\\nuation. In particular, we do not run the\\\\nORCA scheduler in this scenario. Instead, given a batch of re-\\\\nquests, the testing script repeats injecting the same batch into\\\\nthe ORCA engine until all requests in the batch ﬁnishes, mim-\\\\nicking the behavior of the canonical request-level scheduling.\\\\nWe also assume that all requests in the batch have the same\\\\nnumber of input tokens and generate the same number of\\\\noutput tokens. We report the time taken for processing the\\\\nbatch (not individual requests) and compare the result with\\\\nFasterTransformer [4].\\\\nThe second scenario tests the end-to-end performance of\\\\nORCA by emulating a workload. We synthesize a trace of\\\\nclient requests because there is no publicly-available request\\\\ntrace for generative language models. Each request in the syn-\\\\nthesized trace is randomly generated by sampling the number\\\\nof input tokens and a max_gen_tokens attribute, where the\\\\nnumber of input tokens plus max_gen_tokens equals to the\\\\nmax_tokens attribute described in Section 4.2. We assume\\\\nthat all requests continue generation until the number of gen-\\\\nerated tokens reaches max_gen_tokens. In other words, we\\\\nmake the model never emit the “<EOS>” token. This is be-\\\\ncause we have neither the actual model checkpoint nor the\\\\nactual input text so we do not have any information to guess\\\\nthe right timing of the “<EOS>” token generation. Once the\\\\nrequests are generated, we synthesize the trace by setting the\\\\nrequest arrival time based on the Poisson process. To assess\\\\nORCA’s behavior under varying load, we change the Poisson\\\\nparameter (i.e., arrival rate) and adjust the request arrival time\\\\naccordingly.
